raw_response:
I am getting older now, and with only 10.1 mu and two people in the house, I cannot take big risks. I do what is steady. Wheat and maize together are safer for me than trying something new, because if one side is not so good, the other still gives grain and some cash. I watch what the neighbors do, and in our village most people still follow the wheat-maize cycle. Last year the wheat needed water at the key time, and the maize did better when there was enough base fertilizer, so this year I will stay with that way. I cannot spend too much at once because some family labor is away working, so I split fertilizer into two times for both crops. That spreads the money and is also safer if the weather changes. I have well water, but pumping costs money, so I will irrigate at the important stages, not too many times unless the field is really dry.

For wheat, I will plant in early October, around the usual village time, so it can establish before winter. I will use a common improved variety from the local dealer, not the most expensive seed. I will put most of the phosphate and potash and part of the nitrogen before sowing, then topdress around jointing if the wheat looks like it needs strength. I will irrigate about three times if the year is normal: once before winter if the soil is dry, once at jointing, once around grain filling. For maize, after wheat harvest in June, I will not waste time with heavy tillage because the turnaround is too tight and labor is short. I will quickly clear the field and sow hybrid maize. I will put some fertilizer at planting and the rest before the big growth stage. If summer rain is enough, I may only irrigate once, but if it turns dry I will add another watering. I spray only when I see a real problem, especially weeds first, then insects if they come.
